intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: New case. Lin's seminar is on Thursday, and the paper asks whether testing yourself beats re-reading.

intro.speaker: summary
intro.text: No need to read it. I've already summarised it for you.

intro.speaker: mira
intro.text: That's exactly what worries me. Let's check the evidence ourselves.

item.speaker: summary
item.prompt: The Summary's version of the study. One claim goes beyond the evidence — present the passage that shows it.

statements.text: Students who wrote down what they remembered did better a week later.
statements.why: That is what the passage reports.

sourceRefs.quote: One week later the recall group remembered clearly more.

statements.text: Re-reading gave a small edge on the five-minute test.
statements.why: True — the advantage flipped only after a delay.

sourceRefs.quote: Five minutes later the re-reading group did slightly better.

statements.text: So recall practice makes you better at solving new problems.
statements.why: The study only measured memory of the same passage; transfer was not tested.

sourceRefs.quote: Whether it transfers to new problems was not tested in this study.

statements.text: Highlighting counts as re-exposure, not retrieval.
statements.why: The passage lists highlighting with re-reading and summaries.

sourceRefs.quote: Re-reading, highlighting and reviewing a summary put the information in front of you again without asking you to recall it.

hints: Which claim is about something the study never measured?

outro.speaker: mira
outro.text: Case closed. The Summary got the headline right — then claimed more than the study tested.
